claim: Hippocampal place cells fire predominantly when an animal is at one or a few specific places (place fields) of a given space.
source: Spatial information is presumably encoded by hippocampal 'place cells', which fire predominantly when an animal is at one or a few specific places (place fields) of a given space (O'Keefe and Dostrovsky, 1971; McNaughton et al., 1983; Wilson and McNaughton, 1993).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to three foundational studies (O'Keefe and Dostrovsky, 1971; McNaughton et al., 1983; Wilson and McNaughton, 1993).

claim: Path integration of information generated from self-motion is important for hippocampal place cell activity.
source: It is known that path integration of the information generated from self-motion is important for hippocampal place cell activity (Hafting et al., 2005; McNaughton et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to two studies (Hafting et al., 2005; McNaughton et al., 2006).

claim: Visual cues play a pivotal role in place cell activities.
source: In particular, visual cues play a pivotal role in place cell activities (Muller, 1996; Knierim, 2002; Colgin et al., 2008; Ravassard et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to four studies (Muller, 1996; Knierim, 2002; Colgin et al., 2008; Ravassard et al., 2013).

claim: Changing the proximal or distal visual cues alters firing rates and/or firing locations of place cells in a one- or two-dimensional space.
source: For example, changing the proximal or distal visual cues alters firing rates and/or firing locations of place cells in a one- or two-dimensional space (Lee et al., 2004a, 2004b; Leutgeb et al., 2005)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to three studies (Lee et al., 2004a, 2004b; Leutgeb et al., 2005).

claim: Rotation of a salient cue card on the wall of a symmetric open arena evokes an equivalent rotation of place field locations.
source: the rotation of a salient cue card on the wall of a symmetric open arena evokes an equivalent rotation of place field locations (Muller and Kubie, 1987).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Muller and Kubie, 1987.

claim: The visual cortex is connected to the hippocampus via a multi-synaptic pathway involving the associational cortices including the entorhinal cortex.
source: Visual cues are presumably encoded and processed in the visual cortex, which is connected to the hippocampus via a multi-synaptic pathway involving the associational cortices including the entorhinal cortex (Miller and Vogt, 1984; Vaudano et al., 1991; Lavenex and Amaral, 2000; Furtak et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to four studies (Miller and Vogt, 1984; Vaudano et al., 1991; Lavenex and Amaral, 2000; Furtak et al., 2007).

claim: Computational models have shown that hippocampal cells can integrate input from cortical cells encoding visual cues to form a conjunctive response that is location-specific.
source: Computational models have shown that hippocampal cells can integrate input from cortical cells, in particular those encoding visual cues, to form a conjunctive response that is location-specific (de Araujo et al., 2001; Schonfeld and Wiskott, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to two computational modeling studies (de Araujo et al., 2001; Schonfeld and Wiskott, 2015).

claim: Local visual cues influence place field location through entorhinal 'border' cells, whereas distal cues influence place field orientation via entorhinal 'head direction' cells.
source: Alternatively, it is proposed that local visual cues influence place field location through entorhinal 'border' cells, whereas distal cues influence place field orientation via entorhinal 'head direction' cells (Knierim and Hamilton, 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Knierim and Hamilton, 2011.

claim: A total of 852 V1 and 3627 CA1 cells were recorded across all recording days and from all the 15 animals.
source: A total of 852 V1 and 3627 CA1 cells were recorded across all recording days and from all the 15 animals (10 ± 1 V1 cells, 44 ± 2 CA1 cells per day per rat, N = 83 day × rats; see 'Materials and methods' for details).
evidence: The claim is directly stated with specific numbers from the experimental recordings.

claim: The median firing rate of V1 cells was 4.3 Hz.
source: The median firing rate of V1 cells was 4.3 [2.0 9.9] Hz (median and [25% 75%] range values, N = 1501 cell × trajectories)
evidence: The claim is directly stated with specific measurement values from the data.

claim: The median firing rate of CA1 cells was 1.6 Hz.
source: whereas the median rate of CA1 cells was 1.6 [0.97 2.5] Hz (N = 2909).
evidence: The claim is directly stated with specific measurement values from the data.

claim: Many V1 cells dramatically increased their firing rates at specific locations of a trajectory.
source: Many V1 cells also dramatically increased their firing rates at specific locations of a trajectory (Figure 2B–D), as we have shown previously (Ji and Wilson, 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by both the text statement and reference to Figure 2B-D showing examples, as well as a citation to previous work (Ji and Wilson, 2007).

claim: The median spatial information content (SIc) value of V1 cells was 0.17 bits/spike.
source: Although the median SIc value of V1 cells (0.17 [0.085 0.34] bits/spike, N = 1501 cell × trajectories) was relatively small
evidence: The claim is directly stated with specific measurement values from the data.

claim: The median spatial information content (SIc) value of CA1 place cells was 1.6 bits/spike.
source: compared with that of CA1 place cells (1.6 [1.1 2.2] bits/spike, N = 2909; p < 0.0001, ranksum test)
evidence: The claim is directly stated with specific measurement values from the data and statistical test results.

claim: The median SIc of V1 cells was significantly greater than that of shuffled V1 cells.
source: it was significantly greater than that of the shuffled V1 cells (0.061 [0.025 0.13] bits/spike; p < 0.0001; Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical comparison (p < 0.0001) and reference to Figure 2E.

claim: 81% of trajectory-active V1 cells were location-responsive on a trajectory.
source: We found that 81% of trajectory-active V1 cells were location-responsive on a trajectory
evidence: The claim is directly stated with a specific percentage from the data analysis.

claim: 90% of trajectory-active CA1 cells were location-responsive.
source: and for comparison, 90% of the trajectory-active CA1 cells were location-responsive.
evidence: The claim is directly stated with a specific percentage from the data analysis.

claim: Location-responsive V1 cells displayed nearly twice the number of firing fields as CA1 place cells.
source: On average, the location-responsive V1 cells displayed nearly twice the number of firing fields as the CA1 place cells (mean ± SE for V1: 2.9 ± 0.04 per trajectory, N = 1216 cell × trajectories; CA1: 1.5 ± 0.02 per trajectory, N = 2618; p < 0.0001, t-test; Figure 2H).
evidence: The claim is supported by specific quantitative data with statistical test results (p < 0.0001) and reference to Figure 2H.

claim: The average field length of V1 cells was significantly smaller than that of CA1 cells.
source: On the other hand, the average field length of V1 cells was significantly smaller than that of CA1 cells (V1: 37.5 ± 0.3 cm, N = 3521 fields; CA1: 47.2 ± 0.4 cm, N = 3918; p < 0.0001; Figure 2I).
evidence: The claim is supported by specific quantitative data with statistical test results (p < 0.0001) and reference to Figure 2I.

claim: V1 and CA1 field numbers increased close to the food wells.
source: We found that V1 and CA1 fields were not equally distributed along the trajectories, but tended to increase in number close to the food wells, as shown previously for CA1 cells (Dupret et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by the data analysis and a citation to previous work (Dupret et al., 2010).

claim: V1 and CA1 field numbers increased before and after the animals traveled through the corners of the track.
source: V1 and CA1 field numbers also increased before and after the animals traveled through the corners of the track, referred to as landmarks, and decreased as the animals traveled through the long segment between the two middle corners (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 3A,B showing the field distribution patterns.

claim: The numbers of V1 and CA1 fields along the trajectories fluctuated together in a highly correlated fashion for both trajectories.
source: The numbers of V1 and CA1 fields along the trajectories fluctuated together in a highly correlated fashion for both trajectories (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 3C showing the correlated fluctuations.

claim: The cross-correlograms for both trajectories had peaks at a positive position (2 cm) on one running direction and a negative position (−4 cm) on the opposite direction.
source: The cross-correlograms for both trajectories had peaks not exactly at position lag 0, but at a positive position (2 cm, p < 0.0001, Pearson's r) on one running direction and a negative position (−4 cm, p < 0.0001) on the opposite direction (Figure 3D,E)
evidence: The claim is supported by specific quantitative data with statistical test results and reference to Figure 3D,E.

claim: The number of V1 fields fluctuated ahead of the number of CA1 fields consistently on both running directions.
source: meaning that the number of V1 fields fluctuated ahead of the number of CA1 fields consistently on both running directions.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the cross-correlation analysis showing spatial lags.

claim: The 2–4 cm leading distance is equivalent to 60–120 ms of leading time given the mean speed of 35 cm/s.
source: Given the mean speed of 35 cm/s of our rats, the 2–4 cm leading distance is equivalent to 60–120 ms of leading time.
evidence: The claim is calculated from the measured spatial lag and running speed data.

claim: 9.7% of V1 cells were bidirectional.
source: We found that among all trajectory-active cells, 9.7% of V1 cells (N = 75) and 10.4% of CA1 cells (N = 212) were bidirectional
evidence: The claim is directly stated with specific percentages from the data analysis.

claim: 10.4% of CA1 cells were bidirectional.
source: We found that among all trajectory-active cells, 9.7% of V1 cells (N = 75) and 10.4% of CA1 cells (N = 212) were bidirectional
evidence: The claim is directly stated with specific percentages from the data analysis.

claim: The cross-correlogram peak positions of bidirectional V1 cells display a bimodal distribution with two groups around 26 cm and −26 cm.
source: The cross-correlogram peak positions of these bidirectional V1 cells display a bimodal distribution with two groups around 26 cm and −26 cm (Figure 4C)
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 4C showing the bimodal distribution.

claim: The peak positions of bidirectional CA1 cells show a bimodal distribution with two groups around 18 cm and −28 cm.
source: Similarly, the peak positions of CA1 cells also show a bimodal distribution with two groups around 18 cm and −28 cm (Figure 4D).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 4D showing the bimodal distribution.

claim: 997 highly significantly correlated pairs of V1 location-responsive cells and CA1 place cells were obtained with peak correlation times within [−0.2, 0.2] s.
source: Among 22,969 pairs of V1 location-responsive cells and CA1 place cells, we obtained 997 highly significantly correlated pairs (see 'Materials and methods' for definition) with peak correlation times within [−0.2, 0.2] s.
evidence: The claim is directly stated with specific numbers from the data analysis.

claim: The distribution of peak times was significantly biased toward positive values (58% positive, 46% negative).
source: The distribution of these peak times was significantly biased toward positive values (58% positive, 46% negative, p = 0.00017, binomial test; Figure 5D).
evidence: The claim is supported by specific percentages with statistical test results (p = 0.00017) and reference to Figure 5D.

claim: On average, V1 cells led CA1 cells in the time domain.
source: The result indicates that, on average, V1 cells led CA1 cells in the time domain, suggesting the propagation of visual information from V1 to CA1.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the temporal correlation analysis showing positive bias in peak times.

claim: 48% of overlapping pairs were significantly correlated in Δrate.
source: We found that 48% and 23% of the overlapping pairs were significantly correlated in Δrate and ΔCOM (p < 0.05, Pearson's r), respectively.
evidence: The claim is directly stated with specific percentages from the data analysis.

claim: 23% of overlapping pairs were significantly correlated in ΔCOM.
source: We found that 48% and 23% of the overlapping pairs were significantly correlated in Δrate and ΔCOM (p < 0.05, Pearson's r), respectively.
evidence: The claim is directly stated with specific percentages from the data analysis.

claim: The average correlation of all overlapping pairs in Δrate was 0.29 ± 0.01.
source: As a group, the average correlation of all the overlapping pairs were significantly greater than 0, the chance-level correlation, for both Δrate (0.29 ± 0.01, p < 0.0001, t-test; Figure 6D)
evidence: The claim is directly stated with specific values and statistical test results.

claim: The average correlation of all overlapping pairs in ΔCOM was 0.16 ± 0.01.
source: and ΔCOM (0.16 ± 0.01, p < 0.0001; Figure 6D).
evidence: The claim is directly stated with specific values and statistical test results.

claim: Overlapping pairs had significantly higher correlation in Δrate than non-overlapping pairs.
source: We found that the overlapping pairs had significantly higher correlation in Δrate than both non-overlapping (correlation: 0.062 ± 0.003; p < 0.0001, t-test) and non-responsive pairs (−0.023 ± 0.015; p < 0.0001; Figure 6D).
evidence: The claim is supported by specific quantitative data with statistical test results and reference to Figure 6D.

claim: Overlapping pairs had significantly higher correlation in ΔCOM than non-overlapping pairs.
source: Similarly, the overlapping pairs had significantly higher correlation in ΔCOM than non-overlapping (correlation: 0.0005 ± 0.0028; p < 0.0001) and non-responsive pairs (correlation: 0.047 ± 0.020; p < 0.0001; Figure 6D).
evidence: The claim is supported by specific quantitative data with statistical test results and reference to Figure 6D.

claim: The firing rate and COM were modulated by speed and head direction in many V1 and CA1 cells.
source: As expected (Huxter et al., 2003; Saleem et al., 2013), the firing rate and COM were modulated by speed and head direction in many V1 and CA1 cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work (Huxter et al., 2003; Saleem et al., 2013) and reference to Figure 6—figure supplement 4.

claim: The average correlation between the modified Δrate of overlapping V1-CA1 pairs was 0.14 ± 0.009.
source: For the group of overlapping V1-CA1 pairs, the average correlation between the modified Δrate (0.14 ± 0.009) remained significantly greater than 0 (p < 0.0001, t-test)
evidence: The claim is directly stated with specific values and statistical test results.

claim: The average correlation between the modified ΔCOM of overlapping V1-CA1 pairs was 0.13 ± 0.009.
source: Similarly, the average correlation between the modified ΔCOM (0.13 ± 0.009) was also significantly greater than 0 (p < 0.0001)
evidence: The claim is directly stated with specific values and statistical test results.

claim: Behavioral variations cannot fully account for the correlation in the firing rate and COM of overlapping V1-CA1 cell pairs.
source: From these results, we conclude that, behavioral variations cannot fully account for the correlation in the firing rate and COM of overlapping V1-CA1 cell pairs.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the analysis showing significant correlations remain after removing behavioral modulations.

claim: All 4 overlapping pairs of V1 and CA1 cells with bidirectional firing showed the same type of directionality.
source: We found that all the 4 overlapping pairs showed the same type of directionality, but only 5 of the 10 non-overlapping pairs did so whereas the other 5 showed the opposite directionality.
evidence: The claim is directly stated with specific numbers from the data analysis.

claim: V1 firing fields showed much less dynamics at the short-term lap-by-lap time scale than CA1 place fields.
source: Therefore, the analysis indicates that V1 firing fields showed much less dynamics at the short-term lap-by-lap time scale than CA1 place fields.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the analysis of lap-by-lap COM changes shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 5.

claim: There was a significant increase from T1 to T3 in the median overall firing rate of V1 cells (50% increase).
source: First, we found that there was a significant increase from T1 to T3 in the median overall firing rate of V1 cells (50% increase between T1 and T3; p < 0.0001, Kruskal–Wallis test including all data at T1, T2 and T3)
evidence: The claim is supported by specific quantitative data with statistical test results (p < 0.0001).

claim: There was no significant increase in the median firing rate of CA1 cells from T1 to T3.
source: but not in the median firing rate of CA1 cells (3% increase between T1 and T3; p = 0.079; Figure 7A).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical test results (p = 0.079) showing no significant change.

claim: There was a significant increase in the median SMI for both V1 (55% increase) and CA1 cells (39% increase) from T1 to T3.
source: Second, there was a significant increase in the median SMI for both V1 (55% increase between T1 and T3; p < 0.0001) and CA1 cells (39% increase between T1 and T3; p < 0.0001; Figure 7B)
evidence: The claim is supported by specific quantitative data with statistical test results (p < 0.0001).

claim: L4 cells had significantly higher firing rates than both L2/3 and L5/6 cells.
source: The post-hoc pair-wise comparisons revealed that L4 cells had significantly higher firing rates (10.2 [6.5 14.9] Hz) than both L2/3 (3.2 [1.7 7.0] Hz, p < 0.0001, ranksum test) and L5/6 (2.9 [1.8 6.3] Hz, p < 0.0001) cells
evidence: The claim is supported by specific quantitative data with statistical test results (p < 0.0001).

claim: 86% of L2/3 cells were location-responsive.
source: The analysis of SMI shows that 86% of L2/3, 78% of L4, and 70% of L5/6 cells were location-responsive.
evidence: The claim is directly stated with specific percentages from the data analysis.

claim: 78% of L4 cells were location-responsive.
source: The analysis of SMI shows that 86% of L2/3, 78% of L4, and 70% of L5/6 cells were location-responsive.
evidence: The claim is directly stated with specific percentages from the data analysis.

claim: 70% of L5/6 cells were location-responsive.
source: The analysis of SMI shows that 86% of L2/3, 78% of L4, and 70% of L5/6 cells were location-responsive.
evidence: The claim is directly stated with specific percentages from the data analysis.

claim: There was a significant increase in firing rate only in L2/3 cells from T1 to T3 (39% increase).
source: We found a significant increase in firing rate only in L2/3 cells (p = 0.00023, Kruskal–Wallis test comparing all data at T1, T2 and T3; 39% increase between T1 and T3), but not in L4 (p = 0.60; 2.5% increase between T1 and T3) or L5/6 cells (p = 0.10; 2.3% increase between T1 and T3; Figure 8C).
evidence: The claim is supported by specific quantitative data with statistical test results.

claim: There was a significant increase in SMI from T1 to T3 for cells in all layers.
source: However, there was a significant increase in SMI from T1 to T3 for cells in all layers (L2/3: p < 0.0001, 52% increase between T1 and T3; L4: p < 0.0001, 130% increase between T1 and T3; L5/6: p = 0.05, 54% increase between T1 and T3; Figure 8D).
evidence: The claim is supported by specific quantitative data with statistical test results.

claim: A large number of cells in all layers of V1 fire selectively and reliably at specific locations of the track.
source: We have analyzed the firing activities of V1 and CA1 cells in freely moving rats as they ran back and forth on a C-shaped track for food reward. We found that a large number of cells in all layers of V1, like CA1 place cells, fire selectively and reliably at specific locations of the track.
evidence: The claim is a summary statement supported by the data presented throughout the Results section.

claim: Location-responsive V1 cells have multiple, narrow firing fields on a given trajectory of the track.
source: These location-responsive V1 cells have multiple, narrow firing fields on a given trajectory of the track.
evidence: The claim is a summary statement supported by the data on field numbers and sizes.

claim: The precise lap-by-lap fluctuations in the firing rate and firing location of V1 cells are correlated with those of CA1 cells with overlapping firing fields.
source: The precise lap-by-lap fluctuations in the firing rate and firing location of V1 cells are correlated with those of CA1 cells with overlapping firing fields.
evidence: The claim is a summary statement supported by the correlation analysis data.

claim: V1 cells display an experience-dependent change in their location-specificity at the time scale of days.
source: Finally, V1 cells display an experience-dependent change in their location-specificity at the time scale of days.
evidence: The claim is a summary statement supported by the data showing changes across recording days.

claim: V1 cells have location-specific responses to a particular environment and are functionally coupled with the hippocampal place cells encoding the same environment.
source: These results reveal that V1 cells have location-specific responses to a particular environment and are functionally coupled with the hippocampal place cells encoding the same environment.
evidence: The claim is a summary conclusion inferred from the multiple lines of evidence presented.

claim: The hippocampus plays a critical role in spatial memories.
source: Given the critical role of the hippocampus in spatial memories (Scoville and Milner, 1957; Squire, 1992; Eichenbaum et al., 1999; Burgess and O'Keefe, 2003)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to four foundational studies.

claim: V1 location-responsive cells may participate in the formation and storage of spatial memories encoded by hippocampal place cells.
source: these visual cells may also participate in the formation and storage of the spatial memories encoded by hippocampal place cells.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on inference from the observed functional coupling and known role of hippocampus in memory.

claim: V1 neurons are likely driven by the visual cues associated with specific locations on the track.
source: Given what we know about the primary function of V1 neurons in behaving rodents (Yao et al., 2007; Niell and Stryker, 2010; Xu et al., 2012), they are likely driven by the visual cues associated with specific locations on the track, supported by our observation that V1 firing fields are more distributed around the landmarks.
evidence: The claim is inferred from citations to previous work on V1 function and the observed distribution of V1 firing fields around landmarks.

claim: Prospective firing may occur when V1 neurons 'see' landmarks in front of the animal.
source: In particular, prospective firing may occur when V1 neurons 'see' landmarks in front of the animal.
evidence: The claim is speculative, proposing a mechanism for the observed prospective firing pattern.

claim: Retrospective firing may occur as V1 neurons 'see' landmarks behind the animal's head.
source: Retrospective firing may occur as V1 neurons 'see' landmarks behind the animal's head, which is possible because the side-facing eyes of rats have a wide visual field and can see visual stimuli behind or above the head (Wallace et al., 2013)
evidence: The claim is speculative, proposing a mechanism for the observed retrospective firing pattern, supported by a citation about rat visual field.

claim: The landmark information represented by V1 cells can reach the hippocampus via a multi-synaptic pathway.
source: The landmark information represented by the V1 cells can reach the hippocampus via a multi-synaptic pathway, which includes the secondary visual cortex, temporal cortex, perirhinal/postrhinal cortex, and entorhinal cortex (Miller and Vogt, 1984; Vaudano et al., 1991; Lavenex and Amaral, 2000; Furtak et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations describing the anatomical pathway.

claim: V1 location-responsive cells may allow local and distal visual cues to influence CA1 place cell activities.
source: In this way, the V1 location-responsive cells may allow local and distal visual cues to influence CA1 place cell activities (Muller and Kubie, 1987; Lee et al., 2004a, 2004b; Leutgeb et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is speculative, proposing a functional role based on inference and supported by citations.

claim: Spatial representation in the brain may involve a gradual transformation along the anatomical pathway connecting the sensory cortex to the hippocampus.
source: Therefore, it is possible that spatial representation in the brain may involve a gradual transformation along the anatomical pathway connecting the sensory cortex to the hippocampus, which converts a primarily sensory-driven, less reliable spatial response in the sensory cortex to a more precise and robust spatial response in the hippocampus.
evidence: The claim is speculative, proposing a theoretical framework based on the observed differences between V1 and CA1 responses.

claim: Hippocampal place cells encode spatial memory and other types of memories.
source: Hippocampal place cells are believed not just to form a neural representation of space, but encode spatial memory and other type of memories (Eichenbaum et al., 1999; Burgess and O'Keefe, 2003; Ferbinteanu et al., 2006; Knierim at al., 2006; Moser et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to five studies.

claim: A spatial memory trace is encoded not only by hippocampal place cells, but also by cortical cells involved in the transformation.
source: If so, then the gradual transformation of spatial representation also suggests that a spatial memory trace is not only encoded by hippocampal place cells, but also by the cortical cells involved in the transformation, which are presumably distributed in many cortical areas.
evidence: The claim is speculative, proposing a distributed memory encoding mechanism based on inference.

claim: Activity patterns of V1 and CA1 cells during track running are coordinately replayed later during slow-wave sleep.
source: Our previous study shows that activity patterns of V1 and CA1 cells during track running are coordinately replayed later during slow-wave sleep (Ji and Wilson, 2007)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: V1 cells and CA1 place cells functionally interact during the stage of memory formation as animals run a novel track.
source: The current study provides another piece of key evidence that V1 cells and CA1 place cells functionally interact during the stage of memory formation as animals run a novel track for a first week or so.
evidence: The claim is a summary statement supported by the data presented in the study.

claim: The lap-by-lap co-fluctuation between V1-CA1 cell pairs with overlapping firing fields is qualitatively similar to that between pairs of CA1-CA1 place cells with overlapping place fields.
source: In our data, the lap-by-lap co-fluctuation between V1-CA1 cell pairs with overlapping firing fields is qualitatively similar to that between pairs of CA1-CA1 place cells with overlapping place fields.
evidence: The claim is supported by the comparison of correlation data between V1-CA1 and CA1-CA1 pairs.

claim: CA1 place cells with overlapping place fields constitute functional 'cell assemblies' that encode the spatial memory of the animal's environment.
source: Since CA1 place cells with overlapping place fields are believed to constitute functional 'cell assemblies' that encode the spatial memory of the animal's environment (Harris et al., 2003; Dragoi and Buzsaki, 2006)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to two studies.

claim: Overlapping V1 location-responsive cells and hippocampal place cells are part of larger 'cortical-hippocampal assemblies' that encode and store the same spatial memory trace.
source: it is possible that the overlapping V1 location-responsive cells and hippocampal place cells are part of the larger 'cortical-hippocampal assemblies' that encode and store the same spatial memory trace.
evidence: The claim is speculative, proposing an extended assembly concept based on inference from the observed co-fluctuations.

claim: V1 location-specific activities are a substrate for encoding and storing the visual component of long-term spatial memories, and possibly episodic memories.
source: Therefore, we propose that the V1 location-specific activities are a substrate for encoding and storing the visual component of long-term spatial memories, and possibly episodic memories.
evidence: The claim is speculative, proposing a functional role for V1 activities in memory based on the evidence presented.

claim: Fifteen Long-Evans rats were used in the electrophysiological recording experiments.
source: Fifteen Long-Evans rats, all male, 3–6 months old, were used in the electrophysiological recording experiments.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: The C-shaped track was approximately 3 m long and approximately 6 cm wide with 3 cm high walls.
source: The track, made of metal, was ∼3 m long and ∼6 cm wide with 3 cm high walls.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: The recording started on the very first day the animals experienced the track (Day 1) and continued for 2–14 days.
source: The recording started on the very first day the animals experienced the track (Day 1) and continued for 2–14 days, with 20–60 min each day.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Eight animals reached at least Day 7.
source: Eight animals reached at least Day 7.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the Results section.

claim: Both running speed and number of laps per minute reached a stable level on Day 3.
source: Both parameters increased rapidly during the early few days of running and reached a stable level on Day 3 (Figure 1B,C)
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 1B,C showing the behavioral data.

claim: V1 cells were sampled in all layers.
source: V1 cells were sampled in all layers (Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 1D showing recording sites.

claim: 776 V1 cells and 2033 CA1 cells were analyzed that were active on at least one trajectory.
source: In this study, we analyzed 776 V1 cells and 2033 CA1 cells that were active on at least one trajectory (mean firing rate >0.5 Hz).
evidence: The claim is directly stated with specific numbers from the data analysis.

claim: Putative CA1 interneurons (mean rate > 5 Hz) were excluded from the analysis.
source: Putative CA1 interneurons (mean rate > 5 Hz) were excluded.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the Materials and methods section.
